hops.afterHeading: An axon has a supply problem
hops.title: Why a foot that fell asleep fizzes as it wakes up
hops.text: Anyone whose foot has gone numb after sitting cross-legged knows the pins and needles as feeling returns. Pressure on a nerve can disrupt signaling, and sufficiently reduced blood flow can depolarize axons. After ischemia, as blood flow returns, the recovering sodium-potassium pump can hyperpolarize the axon enough to draw in potassium that accumulated outside. That inward potassium current is a proposed trigger for post-ischemic tingling, briefly counteracting hyperpolarization so sensory axons depolarize and fire spontaneously. It likely contributes little to tingling from focal nerve compression. Sensory axons from the skin are more excitable than motor axons and more prone to firing unprompted, so they are the ones that fizz.

sources.citation: Lin et al., The Journal of Physiology 541(3):1025-1039 (2002).
Han et al., The Journal of Physiology 588(10):1737-1745 (2010).

image.caption: Pins and needles can linger briefly as compressed sensory axons recover after pressure is released.

hops.title: Ketones take the side door when GLUT1 is broken
hops.text: Children born with GLUT1 deficiency syndrome have normal glucose in their blood, yet their brains run short of fuel. GLUT1 carries glucose across the brain's blood vessels and into astrocytes, and when it is faulty the result can be seizures and movement difficulties. The standard treatment is a medical ketogenic diet, which has the liver turn fat into ketone bodies. Ketones skip the broken glucose gate: they cross on monocarboxylate transporters such as MCT1, the family that also carries lactate and pyruvate. In a parent survey, 80 percent of patients with seizures were reported to have at least 90 percent fewer on dietary therapy; some respond less well.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A wooden table holding halved avocados, walnuts, olives, cream in a pitcher, and butter on a stoneware plate.
image.caption: When GLUT1 delivers too little glucose, ketone bodies can reach the brain through transporters such as MCT1.

hops.title: Golgi's kitchen laboratory and the first glial feeding idea
hops.text: In June 1872, passed over for a post at the University of Pavia, the physician Camillo Golgi became chief physician at a hospital for incurables in Abbiategrasso and set up a laboratory in his apartment kitchen. There he hardened brain tissue in potassium dichromate, soaked it in silver nitrate, and turned transparent nerve cells stark black: the black reaction. Virchow had described glia in the 1850s as a connective substance holding nerve cells together. Golgi's stain showed star-shaped glia sending end-feet onto blood vessels, and he proposed that they passed nourishment from blood to brain tissue. More than 150 years later, how much they do is still argued over.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An antique brass microscope beside glass jars of stain, glass slides, a teapot, and a lit candle on a rustic kitchen table.
image.caption: An 1870s kitchen laboratory produced the stain that first showed glia reaching for blood vessels.
